Thank you for submitting your article "Mechanisms of Opening and Closing of the Bacterial Replicative Helicase" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Michael R Botchan as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Philip Cole as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Huilin Li (Reviewer #3). A further reviewer remains anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The reviewers all found this manuscript interesting and the conclusions well justified. The contribution is captured by the following summary.

The loading of replicative helicases onto DNA, often assisted by dedicated loader proteins, is an essential step during the initiation of DNA replication. In the manuscript "Mechanisms of Opening and Closing of the Bacterial Replicative Helicase", Chase et al., determine a cryo-EM structure of the E. coli replicative helicase, DnaB, in complex with the helicase loader protein from bacteriophage λ at an average resolution of ~4.1 A. Surprisingly, the structure shows that the DnaB hexamer binds 5 copies of the phage loader protein at its C-terminal side, with each λ P associating with two adjacent DnaB protomers. This unusual stoichiometry is supported by native mass spectrometry. In the BP complex structure, the DnaB hexamer adopts a constricted and spiral conformation that leads to a break in both the NTD and CTD tiers of the DnaB ring. This gap is wide enough to allow ssDNA to enter the central cavity and therefore supports a ring-breaking mechanism for loading of the E. coli replicative helicase. The authors further note that the DnaB ATPase ring is held in a restrained configuration that prevents the DNA binding loops and ATPase centers to adopt a conformation competent for ssDNA binding and ATP hydrolysis, respectively. However, this conformation likely is in some equilibrium with other states (see below for an issue that should be addressed in revisions). Overall these observations lead the authors to propose detailed models for both ring opening and closing of DnaB during replication initiation.

Several crystal structures of DnaB have been determined previously, either in isolation or in complex with ssDNA, but structural information of DnaB-loading intermediates has been limited to a 25 A structure of DnaB in complex with its cognate E. coli loader protein, DnaC. The structure of the BP complex determined by Chase et al. thus represents the first near-atomic resolution structure of a DnaB-loader complex in the pre-loading state. Although the conformation of DnaB in the BP complex structure is very reminiscent of its configuration in the DnaBC complex, the new structure allows the authors to refine existing models for DnaB ring opening and closing and illustrates how two distinct loader proteins can remodel DnaB in a similar manner.

Suggested revisions:

1) The authors find that the inclusion of ssDNA improves the homogeneity of the complex when analyzed by native mass spectrometry and that it eliminates low abundant B6-P4 and B6-P6 assemblies. Moreover, it seems logical to assume that the use of a non-hydrolyzable nucleotide instead of ATP (which is hydrolyzed to ADP in the map) might stabilize the complex further. It is unclear why the authors did not attempt either approach, which may provide a higher resolution structure and would allow for more confident modeling of the λ P protein. Further explanation of the authors' reasoning would be appreciated.

2) The conformation of DnaB in the BP complex seems very similar to its conformation in the E. coli DnaB-DnaC complex. Although the authors acknowledge this in the main text, it would be useful to include this comparison in figure form as well, both for the ATPase domains and the NTDs.

3) In Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, the authors show co-purification of untagged DnaB with the His-tagged C-terminal domain of λ P (aa 103-233) to support that the C-terminal region of λ P binds DnaB. However, this biochemical experiment lacks important controls, including a) a pull-down performed in the absence of His-tagged λ P protein to control for unspecific association of DnaB with beads and b) a pull-down using a tagged N-terminal fragment of λ P, which should not associate with DnaB according to the authors' interpretation. Moreover, the full-length λ P protein and the C-terminal fragment 103-233 both migrate around 20kDa in the gel despite their significantly different molecular weights. It would be helpful if the authors commented on this discrepancy.

4) It is very difficult to identify individual particles in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D. The authors should consider showing a micrograph with better signal to noise and only highlight a few picked particles by circles. In addition, the 8 volumes that resulted from the 3D classification should be shown. There is also a discrepancy in the reported resolution of the cryoET reconstruction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) in the legend and text (40 vs 25 A), which should be clarified.

5) To demonstrate agreement of the built model with the EM map, the authors should provide the FSC comparing model with EM map.

6) Figure 2—figure supplement 5: It is unclear what the authors mean by "heterogeneous" and "homogenous" refinement and, therefore, these approaches should be explained.

7) Figure 6B: The authors' conclusion that the ATPase sites in the BP complex are misaligned is only weakly supported by the data shown. The authors report movements with distances much lower than the resolution of the structure. Although the authors acknowledge that the reported distances are only tentative, this practice is problematic, and we recommend that the authors should remove these distance measurements. In addition, it would be important to show densities for the side chains in the BP complex at the ATPase sites to demonstrate that the positioning of these side chains in the BP model is reliably supported by density in the map. Likewise, the authors should show densities for the bound nucleotide to support their conclusion that five ATPase sites are occupied by ADP instead of ATP.

8) A reviewer was confused about the exact state of the Stage II complex. Because Stage III is the loader-origin-helicase complex, so, Stage II as described in this manuscript should be competent and ready to bind the origin DNA. But in several places, it was stated that the structure does not hydrolyze ATP (ATP binding sites are disrupted) and cannot bind ssDNA (Figure 6) (subsection “The DNA and ATP binding sites are disrupted in the DnaB• λP complex”). This seems to conflict with the mass spec data indicating the structure's ability to bind a 43-mer ori-lamda ssDNA (Figure 3D), and the fact that five ADP molecules occupy the structure – meaning the structure has hydrolyzed ATP. This issue is alluded to in the summary- with a potential resolution? If the reported structure is indeed incompatible with DNA binding, does this mean the structure is a non-functional structure not found in a cell or perhaps a minor conformation in the cell?

9) Related to the point in 8), the native mass spec shows the formation of DnaB-loader P-43-mer DNA (Figure 3D). Did the authors attempt to visualize the structure, and if yes, is DNA visible, and is the structure distinct from the one reported here which is in the absence of DNA?

10) Native mass spec revealed three species 6:5 (dominant), 6:4, and 6:6 stoichiometric binding. Did the authors identify the two non-dominant species (B6P4 and B6P6) in their 3D classification scheme of the cryo-EM dataset?

results.result: The structure of the E. coli DnaB helicase•bacteriophage λP helicase loader complex (BP complex) was determined to 4.1 Å resolution using cryo-EM and tomography. The structure reveals six DnaB protomers with five of six nucleotide-binding sites occupied by ADP, and five copies of λP helicase loader. The unanticipated B6P5 stoichiometry was verified by native mass spectrometry, which showed a predominant species at 446.3 kDa. Addition of origin-derived ssDNA eliminated compositional heterogeneity, yielding a single B6P5•ssDNA complex at 459.5 kDa. Surprisingly, no nucleotide was detected by native MS despite ATP being present in samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C33 are well-supported by convergent structural (cryo-EM at 4.1 Å), biochemical (native MS), and orthogonal validation methods (CX-MS). The resolution is sufficient for unambiguous placement of DnaB protomers and identification of five λP molecules. Native MS independently confirms the B6P5 stoichiometry and ssDNA binding. The discrepancy between cryo-EM (showing ADP) and native MS (showing no nucleotide) is acknowledged but does not undermine the core structural findings.

results.result: The BP complex adopts a three-layered architecture (135 Å x 150 Å x 120 Å) with NTD and CTD layers of DnaB in a right-handed open spiral configuration, distinct from all previously described DnaB structures but reminiscent of the low-resolution E. coli DnaB•DnaC complex. The λP loader, combined with breached interfaces in both layers, creates a ~90-100 Å canyon open to solvent that could accommodate ~30 bp of DNA, consistent with measurements on the analogous DnaB•DnaC complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C34-C42 are supported by direct structural measurements from the 4.1 Å cryo-EM structure. The dimensions, layer organization, and spiral configuration are clearly defined. The comparison to the low-resolution DnaB•DnaC structure (C38) is appropriately qualified as 'reminiscent.' The DNA accommodation estimate (C41-C42) is reasonable based on structural dimensions and comparison with prior work, though it remains an inference rather than direct observation.

results.result: Five λP protomers bind at consecutive DnaB subunit interfaces, with each λP helical domain binding in a gulley between adjacent DnaB CTDs. The λP protomers form a right-handed spiral with ~3.1 Å rise per subunit and ~10 Å pitch. Each λP sends a lasso-like segment along the CTD edge, and two λP protomers (λP2 and λP4) contact nearby NTDs, creating two types of λP-DnaB interfaces. The BP complex is organized around five λP•(DnaB)2 heterotrimers, each burying ~2200-2600 Å² of surface area. This extensive 'molecular handcuffing' of two flanking DnaB subunits by each λP is consistent with high affinity binding and likely prevents conformational changes required for translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C53 are well-supported by the cryo-EM structure and helical parameter analysis. The binding mode, interface types, and buried surface areas are directly measured from the structure. The inference about 'molecular handcuffing' preventing translocation (C52-C53) is reasonable based on the structural constraints observed and is consistent with prior biochemical data showing λP inhibits DnaB activity. The buried surface area values are appropriately noted as lower limits due to incomplete λP modeling.

results.result: The CTD layer in the BP complex adopts an open right-handed spiral staircase configuration, distinct from the closed planar ring forms (dilated and constricted) of isolated DnaB and the hybrid arrangement of the ssDNA-bound complex. The CTDs exhibit a helical rise of ~4.1 Å, pitch of ~16 Å, and twist of ~56.4° (compared to ~7.4 Å rise, ~27 Å pitch, and ~60° twist in the ssDNA complex). The CTDs are inclined ~20° toward the helical axis compared to the dilated form, bringing them close to (but not identical to) the configuration required for ATP hydrolysis. The inner chamber diameter is ~20-25 Å (constricted configuration), comparable to the ssDNA complex but much smaller than the dilated form (~50 Å). Reconfiguration involves three changes: (1) displacements along the helical axis (~40% shorter pitch than ssDNA complex), (2) underwinding by ~3.6°, and (3) inclination toward the helical axis. These changes rupture one CTD interface (between subunits A and B), creating a ~15 Å gap large enough for ssDNA entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C73 are strongly supported by detailed helical parameter analysis and structural comparisons with prior DnaB structures. The measurements are precise and internally consistent. The comparisons across different DnaB forms (Stage I, II/III, IV) are justified by high sequence and structural conservation (C57). The inference that the ~15 Å gap permits ssDNA entry (C73) is reasonable based on the dimensions. The claim that CTDs are 'close but not identical' to the catalytically competent configuration (C62) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: The λP loader induces a DnaB conformation that is neither optimal for DNA binding nor ATP hydrolysis. Although λP binds >10 Å from both ATP and DNA-binding sites, it indirectly disrupts these sites through structural changes. Alterations in CTD helical pitch, twist, and inclination distort DNA-binding loops, shifting key residues by ~3-18 Å compared to the ssDNA complex. Five of six nucleotide-binding sites are occupied by ADP (the sixth site at the breached interface is empty), but the sites are remodeled into a configuration likely not optimal for catalysis. Key residues (K440, R442) are shifted away from positions seen in the active ssDNA complex. These distortions are consistent with prior biochemical data showing λP suppresses DnaB ATPase and helicase activities and prevents crosslinking between DnaB and origin-derived ssDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C89 are well-supported by structural analysis and comparison with the active ssDNA complex, corroborated by prior biochemical data (C74, C75, C88). The inference that suppression arises indirectly through structural changes (C77) is logical given the >10 Å distance between λP and active sites (C76). The measurements of DNA-binding loop shifts (C80) and nucleotide site distortions (C82-C85) are directly from the structure. The authors appropriately note that small structural changes should be considered tentative at 4.1 Å resolution and that absence of ATP may contribute to sub-optimal alignment.

results.result: Despite minimal direct contacts between λP and the NTD tier, the NTD layer is reconfigured into an open spiral arrangement. The likely driver is λP-enforced remodeling of the CTD tier, which provides a reconfigured surface for NTD packing. The NTD layer maintains a trimer-of-dimers configuration with conserved dimers (RMSD 1.3 Å), but the arrangement of dimers is distinct from other DnaB structures. The NTD layer adopts a constricted state (~20-25 Å diameter) with helical parameters (rise ~2.6 Å, pitch ~7 Å, twist ~40-70°) similar to the ssDNA complex. Reconfiguration creates a ~20 Å gap at the disrupted interface, sufficient for ssDNA access. The relationship between NTD and CTD layers changes: the angle between layers is ~15° in the BP complex (vs. ~7° in Stage IV and essentially parallel in closed planar forms), and buried surface area decreases from ~7100 Å² (closed ring) to ~3100 Å² (BP complex), indicating looser association.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C116 are well-supported by structural analysis. The allosteric mechanism (C92, C106, C115) is a reasonable inference based on the structural relationship between CTD and NTD layers and the minimal direct λP-NTD contacts. The helical parameter analysis (C102-C103) and structural comparisons (C94-C98) are rigorous. The measurements of inter-layer angle (C108-C110) and buried surface area (C111-C113) are direct from the structure. The inference that reduced buried surface area indicates looser association (C113) is standard structural interpretation.

results.result: Opening the DnaB helicase requires five λP loaders binding to consecutive interfaces; the ruptured sixth interface cannot bind a sixth loader. The closed ring form of DnaB harbors two types of NTD interfaces (tail-to-tail and head-to-tail), with the tail-to-tail interface likely requiring more energy to open. The breached interface in the BP complex is the weaker head-to-tail interface. The authors speculate that individual loaders could bind stochastically, with each binding event remodeling an interface until five have bound.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are supported by the structure showing five λP molecules and structural analysis of interface types. The inference about differential energetics of the two interface types (C119) is reasonable based on structural features and prior studies. However, C121 is explicitly speculative and lacks direct experimental support. The overall result is supported by structural data, but the mechanism of sequential binding remains hypothetical.

results.result: Reconfiguration of the helicase by λP produces openings (~15 Å in CTD layer, ~20 Å in NTD layer) large enough to admit ssDNA into the inner chamber. The helicase is observed in a restrained inactive configuration with distorted ATP-binding and DNA-binding sites that poises it to close upon receiving an activating signal and transition to the translocation state.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 are supported by structural measurements showing the gap sizes and distorted active sites. The inference that these openings are 'large enough' for ssDNA entry is reasonable based on the dimensions. The characterization as 'restrained inactive' and 'poised to close' is supported by the structural proximity to the active conformation and the observed distortions. However, the actual mechanism of activation and closing requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Activation of DnaB for translocation requires eviction of λP and sealing of breaches in NTD and CTD layers. Prior work documents that the DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE chaperone apparatus engages at the lambda origin to dissolve λP from the BP complex. The authors infer that eviction allows the CTD tier to relax to its full helical pitch (~27 Å) and adopt a ~60° helical twist, freeing DNA-binding and ATPase sites to assume productive conformations. They speculate that: (1) ssDNA entry could drive closure forward to the spiral form rather than backward to the planar form, (2) λP expulsion enables ADP-to-ATP exchange, (3) the unfilled nucleotide site at the breached interface will bind ATP to promote closing, and (4) the freed CTD tier can undergo conformational changes expected during translocation.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is a reasonable inference based on structural differences between BP and active helicase. Claim C123 is supported by prior literature. However, claims C124-C131 are largely speculative inferences about the closing mechanism based on structural comparisons. While these speculations are logical and consistent with the structural data, they lack direct experimental validation. The proposed mechanisms (C128-C130) are explicitly speculative. Additional experiments (e.g., time-resolved structural studies, mutational analysis) would be needed to validate these mechanistic proposals.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on bacterial helicase assembly, establishing that: (1) bacterial replicative helicases are closed hexameric rings that require specialized loading factors for assembly on ssDNA, (2) the architecture and translocation mechanisms of helicases are well-studied, but less is known about opening, assembly, and closing, (3) assembly occurs during replication initiation involving four elements (origin DNA, initiator protein, helicase, loader), and (4) the assembly pathway has at least four stages (isolated helicase, helicase•loader complex, helicase•loader•DNA complex, active helicase).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C22 are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature and represent established knowledge in the field. These claims provide essential context for the current work and are appropriately referenced. The four-stage assembly pathway framework (C15) is supported by prior studies and provides a useful conceptual model for interpreting the current structural findings.
